newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST-Televisa Q1 earnings seen strong.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Televisa Q1 earnings seen strong.

text.p: Mexican media empire Grupo Televisa is likely to consolidate its recovery from a sluggish 1996 when it posts first quarter earnings this year, analysts said.

A survey of three analysts showed they predicted average earnings per ordinary CPO share of 0.24 pesos for the first quarter. The estimates varied widely, from 0.03 to 0.36 pesos, but all were positive, in contrast to the loss of 1.60 pesos per share posted in the same period last year.
"The quarterly results should be good and they would be well received by the market," Pablo Riveroll, an analyst with Merrill Lynch in Mexico City, wrote in a recent report.
The results were "expected to confirm a turnaround", Riveroll added.
Analysts said earnings, due to be reported by April 30, would be driven by the company's television division, the largest in the Spanish-speaking world.

Greater advertising revenue from competing long-distance telephone operators and pension fund administrators was expected to offset the loss of domestic television ratings to rival TV Azteca, they added.
The publishing division was expected to post appreciable increases in earnings over a slow first quarter in 1996, while radio and cable TV earnings were expected to grow more modestly.
Analysts said comparing first quarter results to those from the fourth quarter was not valid in Televisa's case because of the company's highly seasonal ad revenue.

The main news during the quarter was the retirement of Televisa founder Emilio Azcarraga Milmo, known as "The Tiger", on March 3 after heading the group since 1972. This was followed by his sudden death on April 16.
Azcarraga Milmo's 29-year old heir, Emilio Azcarraga Jean, took over as president and chief executive officer while Guillermo Canedo White was named chairman of the board and chief corporate officer.
Stock market traders noted the share price did stumble briefly on news of Azcarraga Milmo's death, but felt long-term effects would be limited.

"We had thought his (Azcarraga Jean's) father would be behind him, so the death came as a shock at first, but the market had already had time to get used to the new team running things," a desk trader said.
For Martin Lara, of Caspian Securities in Mexico City, the new Televisa management did not represent an unsettling break with the past.
"With the namings (of Azcarraga Jean and Canedo White in March), the new administration is pretty much intact and there is continuity," he said.
